summary: This unit teaches you to join metals by brazing and silver soldering, where a filler metal melts and flows into the joint but the parts themselves do not melt. You will learn to work safely with gas torches, fluxes and fumes; set up, light and shut down oxy-acetylene and air-LPG equipment; choose fillers and fluxes; prepare, heat and braze copper pipe and thin steel joints; and clean, inspect, test and report on your work.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It teaches **brazing** and **silver soldering**: joining metal parts with a filler metal that melts at a lower temperature than the parts, so that the parts are heated but never melted.

Brazing is everywhere in Jamaica once you look for it. Plumbers and air-conditioning technicians silver braze copper water pipes and refrigerant lines in houses, hotels and offices. Fabricators braze thin steel tube for furniture and frames, repair cast iron and join galvanised parts with brass rod. Toolmakers and jewellers silver solder small, fine parts. Because brazing uses less heat than welding, it is the right choice for thin parts, for joining two different metals and for neat, leak-tight pipe joints.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres. You will work with copper tube and fittings, thin mild steel sheet, silver brazing alloys, brass brazing rods and their fluxes, using oxy-acetylene and air-LPG torches.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Work safely
Control the hazards of flames, hot metal, fumes from fluxes and fillers, and gas cylinders; wear the right PPE; prevent fires; give first aid for burns.
Plan the job
Read the drawing and job sheet; choose the process, the filler, the flux and the torch for the metals and the joint.
Set up and use the gas equipment
Check and assemble the cylinders, regulators, arrestors, hoses and torch; leak-test; light the torch and set the right flame.
Prepare the joint
Design or check the joint gap and overlap; cut, deburr and clean the parts; put on the flux; hold the parts in line.
Braze and silver solder
Heat the parts evenly, read the flux, feed the filler at the right moment, control the heat on thick and thin parts, and keep the joint still while it sets.
Clean, inspect and test
Wash off the flux, check the joint for a full, even fillet, name the faults and their causes, and carry out a water test or a peel test.
Finish and report
Shut down the gas safely, store the materials, put waste in the right bin, and report faults, damage and incidents.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the principles of brazing, safety, gas equipment, fillers, fluxes, joint design, heating, faults and testing.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade words such as wetting, inner cone, borax and braze welding) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: silver brazing a small copper pipe assembly and water-testing it, and brass brazing lap joints in thin mild steel sheet, then peeling a joint apart to see how far the filler ran. The assessor watches how you work, not only the finished joint.

blocks.note: The written paper often asks you to compare processes, describe a method step by step, or name faults with their causes and cures. Practise saying each method out loud in the right order.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: How brazing and silver soldering work

blocks.p: In fusion welding, the edges of the parts melt and run together with the filler into one pool. In brazing, the **parent metal** (the metal of the parts) does **not** melt. Only the **filler metal** melts. It flows over the hot, clean surfaces, is drawn into the joint, then sets and bonds to them.

The difference between brazing and soldering is the melting temperature of the filler. Fillers that melt **above about 450 °C** are brazing fillers. Fillers that melt below about 450 °C are soft solders, and the process is **soft soldering**.

Soft soldering
Silver soldering (silver brazing)
Brass brazing and braze welding
rows: Filler
Tin-based solder (lead-free for drinking-water pipe)
Silver-bearing brazing alloy (silver, copper, zinc and sometimes tin)
Brass rod, about 60% copper and 40% zinc, sold as "bronze" brazing rod
Filler melts
Below 450 °C, often about 180–250 °C
Above 450 °C, typically about 600–800 °C
About 870–900 °C
Usual heat source
Soldering iron or small air-gas torch
Air-LPG torch, or oxy-acetylene with a soft flame
Oxy-acetylene
Flux
Soldering flux
Silver brazing flux, usually a white paste
Borax-type flux, or flux-coated rods
Strength
Weak: for sealing and light loads
Strong, neat joints in close-fitting parts
Strong; fills wider gaps and builds up fillets
Typical jobs
Electrical connections, light sheet work, some small pipe
Copper water pipe, air-conditioning and refrigeration lines, brass fittings, small steel parts, fine work
Thin steel tube and frames, cast iron repairs, galvanised parts

blocks.note: **Silver soldering** is the trade name for **silver brazing**. The filler melts above 450 °C, so it is brazing, not soft soldering, even though it is called soldering.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When two clean surfaces are very close together, a liquid is pulled into the narrow gap between them. This is **capillary action**: the same effect that draws water up a thin straw or into the gap between two wet sheets of glass. In a close-fitting brazed joint, capillary action pulls the melted filler right through the joint, sideways and even upwards, whichever way up the joint is.
Capillary action only works when four things are right:

ul: The **gap** is small and even all round, a fraction of a millimetre.
The surfaces are **clean**: no grease, paint, rust or oxide.
The right **flux** covers the surfaces and keeps oxide away.
**Both** parts are at brazing temperature at the same time.

blocks.p: **Wetting** is the melted filler spreading out in a thin, even film and sticking to the metal, the way water spreads over a clean plate. On dirty, oxidised or cold metal it does not wet: it forms round beads that sit on the surface, the way water beads up on a greasy plate. A filler that has not wetted the surface has not bonded to it.

In true brazing, the filler is drawn into a close-fitting joint by capillary action. In **braze welding** (also called bronze welding), a brass rod is used to build up a fillet or fill a V-shaped groove, like a weld bead, without relying on capillary flow. The parent metal still does not melt. Braze welding is used to repair cast iron, to join galvanised tube and to build up worn parts.

head: Advantages
Limits
rows: Less heat than welding, so less distortion and less risk of melting thin parts
Joins different metals: copper to brass, copper to steel, steel to brass
Joins thin parts to thick ones
Neat, leak-tight joints in pipe
A joint can be taken apart again by reheating it
The joint is only strong if it is well designed, usually as a lap or sleeve
Not for parts that will run very hot: the filler softens at a much lower heat than the parent metal
The filler's colour may not match the parts
Flux residue must be removed
Silver alloys are costly, so they must not be wasted

blocks.p: Brazing has five main hazards: **burns**, **fire**, **fumes**, **glare** from the flame and the glowing joint, and the **gases** in the cylinders. Look at the job and the area before you light up, and decide how you will control each one.

head: Hazard
What can happen
How you control it
rows: Burns
An oxy-acetylene flame is over 3 000 °C. Parts stay hot long after they stop glowing, and hot flux can spit.
Leather gloves and all skin covered
Tongs or pliers for hot parts
Hot parts marked HOT
Torch hung up, never laid down lit
Fire
The flame and hot parts set fire to wood, paper, rags, ceiling boards, plastic trunking and pipe insulation. On site the danger is often behind or above the joint.
Anything that burns moved or shielded
Work on firebricks or a heat-resistant mat
Extinguisher at hand
Area checked for smouldering afterwards
Fumes

Hot flux gives off fumes that irritate the eyes, nose and lungs. Brass rod and brass parts give off **zinc** fume, which causes metal fume fever. Older silver alloys can contain **cadmium**, whose fume is very toxic and can cause severe lung damage, even death.
Good ventilation or extraction
Head kept out of the fumes
Cadmium-free fillers only
No overheating
Respirator where the instructor says
Glare
The flame and the glowing flux are very bright. They strain the eyes and hide the joint, and sparks and spitting flux can hit the eyes.
Tinted goggles or a visor of about shade 3 to 5
Gases
A leak of fuel gas can catch fire or explode. Extra oxygen in the air makes clothing burn fiercely. A flame can burn back into the equipment.
Equipment checked and leak-tested
Flashback arrestors and check valves fitted
Cylinders upright and secured
Good ventilation

head: PPE
What it protects you from
Points to check
rows: Gas welding goggles or a visor with a filter of about shade 3 to 5
Glare, heat, sparks and spitting flux
Filter not cracked
Fits well; strap sound
An arc welding helmet (shade 10 to 13) is far too dark for brazing: you could not see the flux change
Clear safety glasses
Chips and burrs when cutting, deburring and cleaning, and splashes of hot water and flux when washing
Side shields fitted
Leather gloves
Heat, hot metal and flux
Dry and without holes
Thinner leather gloves give better feel for fine silver soldering, but must still be heat-resistant
Long-sleeved cotton or wool clothing, or a leather jacket or apron
Heat, sparks and spitting flux on the skin
Buttoned at the neck and cuffs
No nylon or polyester: they melt onto the skin
Free of oil and grease
Safety boots
Dropped parts and cylinders, hot metal
Trousers worn over the boots
Respirator
Fumes where ventilation or extraction is not enough
The type the safety data sheet or your instructor names

ul: Read the **safety data sheet (SDS)** for each flux and filler. The supplier must provide one. It gives the hazards, the PPE to wear and the first aid to give.
Many brazing fluxes contain **fluorides** and boron compounds. Their fumes irritate, and the paste irritates skin and eyes. Wear gloves and wash your hands before you eat, drink or smoke.
Use only **cadmium-free** silver brazing alloys. If you find old stock marked "contains cadmium", do not use it: give it to your instructor.

**White smoke** rising from brass rod or a brass part is zinc boiling off. It is a sign that you are overheating, and the fume causes **metal fume fever**: shivers, fever, aches and sickness, like flu, a few hours later.
Work where air moves through the bay, or with extraction close to the joint. Keep your face out of the rising fumes. On site, stand so the breeze carries the fumes away from you.
Never braze galvanised, painted or plated parts without removing the coating from the joint area and using extraction.
At the Centre, braze on a **brazing hearth** or on firebricks, so that the flame and hot parts cannot reach the bench.
Clear away anything that can burn. If it cannot be moved, shield it with a fire-resistant blanket or a heat shield placed behind the joint.
Keep a suitable extinguisher at hand and know how to use it.
Never leave a lit torch lying on the bench. Hang it up or turn it off.
After the job, check the area, including behind and above the work, for smoke or smouldering before you leave.

blocks.note: Many brazing jobs are done inside homes, hotels and offices, where air-conditioning lines run close to ceiling boards, wooden window frames, curtains and plastic trunking. Put a heat shield behind every joint, keep an extinguisher by you, and check the area again before you leave the site.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Cool the burn under cool running water straight away, for at least 10 minutes (20 is better)
Take off rings, watches and tight clothing near the burn, unless they are stuck to it
Cover it loosely with a clean, non-fluffy dressing or cling film
Do not put butter, oil, ice or toothpaste on it, and do not burst blisters
Get medical help for a large or deep burn, or a burn to the face, hands or eyes
Tell your instructor and record it in the accident book

blocks.note: In an emergency in Jamaica, dial 110 for fire and ambulance.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Gas equipment: setting up and lighting

blocks.p: Two kinds of torch are used for brazing. An **oxy-acetylene** torch burns acetylene with pure oxygen from a cylinder. Its flame is the hottest (over 3 000 °C at the tip of the inner cone), and it is used for brass brazing steel and for bigger silver brazing jobs. An **air-fuel** torch burns **LPG** (liquefied petroleum gas: propane or butane, the same as household cooking gas) with air drawn in at the torch. Its flame is cooler, about 1 900 °C, but it is simple and portable, and it is widely used for silver soldering small copper pipe.

blocks.h: The parts of an oxy-acetylene set

head: Part
Its job
Check before use
rows: Oxygen cylinder
Holds oxygen at a very high pressure (often 150–200 bar or more when full)
Upright and chained
Valve outlet clean and free of oil and grease
Acetylene cylinder
Holds acetylene dissolved in acetone, soaked into a porous filling inside
Always upright and chained
Valve key kept on the valve while in use
Regulators
Reduce the high cylinder pressure to a low, steady working pressure. The contents gauge shows the cylinder pressure; the working gauge shows the pressure going to the torch.
Right regulator for the gas
Threads clean and undamaged
Gauge glasses whole
Flashback arrestors
Fitted at the regulator outlets. They stop a flame travelling back through the hoses to the regulators and cylinders.
Fitted on both gases, in date and undamaged
Hoses
Carry the gases to the torch. The fuel gas hose is **red**; the oxygen hose is **blue** (green on some American equipment).
No cracks, cuts, burns or soft spots
Clips or ferrules tight
Check valves (non-return valves)
Fitted where the hoses join the torch. They let gas flow one way only, so the gases cannot mix in the hoses.
Fitted to both inlets
Torch (blowpipe) and nozzle
The torch mixes the gases; the nozzle size sets the size of the flame
Nozzle the right size from the maker's chart
Nozzle hole clean and round; seat undamaged
Spark lighter
Lights the torch safely, at arm's length
Flint sparks well

blocks.note: Fuel gas fittings have **left-hand threads**, and their nuts usually have a notch or groove cut round them. Oxygen fittings have right-hand threads. This stops the hoses being connected to the wrong gas. Never force a fitting that will not turn easily.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Never let oil or grease touch oxygen cylinders, valves, regulators or hoses, and never handle them with oily gloves: oil and grease can catch fire or explode in pure oxygen. Never use oxygen to blow dust off your clothes or to cool yourself: clothing full of oxygen bursts into flame from a spark.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Acetylene becomes unstable at high pressure. Never set its working pressure above about **1 bar (15 psi)**.

Keep acetylene cylinders **upright**, in use and in store, so the acetone stays in the cylinder and cannot come out through the valve. If one has been lying down, stand it upright and leave it for the time the gas supplier says before you use it.
Open the acetylene cylinder valve slowly, **less than one and a half turns**, and leave the key on it so it can be shut quickly in an emergency.
LPG is **heavier than air**. A leak sinks and collects in drains, pits and low corners, where a spark can set it off. Keep LPG cylinders upright, in a ventilated place, away from drains and pits.
Cylinder colours differ between suppliers and countries. Read the label on the cylinder; never go by its colour alone.

flow: Check that both cylinders are upright and chained, and that the labels show the right gases
Check that the valve outlets and regulator threads are clean, undamaged and free of oil
Fit the oxygen regulator (right-hand thread) and the fuel regulator (left-hand thread), and tighten them with the correct spanner
Fit a flashback arrestor to each regulator outlet
Check the hoses, then connect them the right way round, with check valves at the torch
Fit the nozzle size the maker's chart gives for the job
Wind out both regulator adjusting screws, stand to one side, and open the cylinder valves slowly
Set the working pressures from the chart, keeping acetylene below about 1 bar (15 psi)
Brush leak-detection fluid or soapy water on every joint and look for bubbles
Purge each hose for a few seconds, one gas at a time, in open air away from flames

blocks.p: **Purging** clears air, or a mixture of the two gases, out of the hoses. A mixture left in a hose can burn back when the torch is lit.

blocks.note: Never look for a leak with a flame, and never seal a leaking hose with tape. If a joint bubbles, close the cylinder valves, bleed the gas off, then tighten or replace the part and test again. A damaged part is tagged out of use and reported.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Lighting the torch and setting the flame

flow: Check the area is clear, put on your PPE, and point the torch away from people, hoses and cylinders
Open the fuel valve on the torch a little and light the gas with a **spark lighter**, never a match or a cigarette lighter
Open the fuel a little more, until the flame stops giving off black smoke
Open the oxygen valve slowly: the long white feather round the inner cone shrinks
Stop when the flame is right for the job: a neutral flame when the feather just disappears into the inner cone

head: Flame
What it looks like
Use in brazing
rows: Carburising (reducing)
A white feather of unburnt acetylene round the bright **inner cone**; the more acetylene, the longer the feather
A **slightly** reducing, soft flame is used for silver brazing copper; a strongly carburising flame leaves soot and is not used
Neutral
A clear, sharp, rounded inner cone with no feather; equal amounts of the two gases burn
Silver brazing, and general heating
Oxidising
A short, pointed inner cone and a hissing sound; extra oxygen
Many instructors use a **slightly** oxidising flame for brass rod on steel, because it cuts down zinc fuming; it blackens and spoils copper

blocks.p: The hottest point of the flame is just beyond the tip of the inner cone. For brazing, keep the inner cone clear of the work and let the larger outer flame spread the heat. The inner cone held on one spot puts far too much heat there.

head: Event
What happens
What to do
rows: Backfire
A loud pop as the flame goes into the nozzle; the flame goes out or relights. Common causes: the nozzle touching the work, an overheated or dirty nozzle, or pressures set too low.
Close the torch valves, check and clean the nozzle, let it cool, check the pressures, then relight
Flashback
The flame burns back inside the torch and towards the hoses, with a squealing or hissing sound; the torch handle gets hot and black smoke may come from the nozzle.
Close the torch valves at once (oxygen first, or as the maker says), then both cylinder valves; let it cool; report it, and do not use the set until it has been checked

blocks.note: Many Jamaican workshops and homes use LPG for cooking, and air-LPG torches use the same gas. Treat a torch cylinder like a cooking-gas cylinder: upright, in fresh air, away from drains, with a regulator and hose made for that gas, and never left with its valve open after the job.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A filler metal must **melt at a lower temperature than the parent metal**, wet it, and give a joint strong enough for the job. Use the filler that the drawing or the job sheet names; if it does not name one, ask.

head: Filler
What it is
Melts at about
Use it on
Points to know
rows: Silver brazing alloy (cadmium-free)
Silver, copper and zinc, sometimes with tin; often 20–56% silver
600–800 °C (more silver usually means a lower, more fluid melt)
Copper, brass, steel, stainless steel, and mixed pairs such as copper to steel
Needs silver brazing flux
Flows into very close gaps
Costly: use only what the joint needs
Copper-phosphorus alloy (with or without a little silver)
Copper and phosphorus; some grades have up to about 15% silver
Copper to copper, with **no flux**; copper to brass **with** flux
The phosphorus cleans copper as it melts, so it acts as its own flux on copper
**Never** use it on steel, cast iron or nickel alloys: it makes a brittle joint
Brass brazing rod ("bronze" rod)
About 60% copper and 40% zinc, often with a little tin or silicon
Mild steel, cast iron, galvanised steel, copper
Needs a borax-type flux, or flux-coated rods
Fills wider gaps and builds up fillets
Used for braze welding
Soft solder (for comparison)
Mainly tin
Below 450 °C
Light jobs only
This is soldering, not brazing

blocks.note: True **bronze** is copper mixed with **tin**. The rods sold as "bronze" brazing rods are mostly copper and **zinc**, which is **brass**. The trade uses both names, so learn both facts.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Fillers come as rods, coils of wire, thin strip, rings that sit inside a fitting, and pastes. Keep them in their packets, labelled, so that one alloy is never mistaken for another: many silver alloys look alike.
When metal is heated in air, a thin skin of **oxide** forms on it: copper goes dark, steel turns blue and then black. Melted filler will not wet or bond to oxide. A flux:

ul: **dissolves** the oxide that is already there,
**covers** the surface so that no new oxide forms while it is heated,
helps the filler **flow** and wet the surface, and
**shows you the temperature**: it changes as the joint heats up.

head: Flux
Use it with
Points to know
rows: Silver brazing flux, usually a white paste
Silver brazing alloys on copper, brass, steel and stainless steel
Works in the silver brazing range, roughly 550–800 °C
Contains fluorides: the fumes irritate and the residue is corrosive
Borax-type brazing flux, a white powder or paste, or a coating on the rod
Brass ("bronze") rods
Works at the higher heat of brass brazing
Leaves a hard, glassy residue
No flux
Copper-phosphorus filler on copper to copper
Use flux as soon as brass or another metal is in the joint

flow: Cold: a white paste
As it warms, the water in it boils off: it bubbles and dries to a white, chalky crust
Near brazing heat (about 600 °C) it **turns clear and runs like water**: the joint is ready for the filler
Overheated, or heated too long: it goes dark green or **black**, stops working, and the filler will not flow

ul: Put flux on **clean** metal only. Flux cannot make up for dirt and grease.
Brush a **thin, even coat** just where the filler must flow: for a socket joint, on the outside of the tube end, with a light smear inside the socket.
Do not fill the joint with flux. Thick lumps get trapped inside as flux inclusions, and filler flows wherever flux is, including where you do not want it.
With brass rod in powder flux, heat the end of the rod and dip it in the powder so the flux sticks, or use flux-coated rods.
Keep the lid on the pot and use a clean brush, so the flux stays clean and does not dry out.

blocks.note: Flux paste and residue irritate the skin and eyes. Wear gloves, keep your hands away from your face, and wash them after the job. If flux gets into an eye, rinse it with plenty of clean water as the safety data sheet says, and tell your instructor.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A brazed joint is only as good as its design and its preparation. Most of the faults found in brazed joints start here, before the torch is lit.

head: Joint
How good for brazing
Points to know
rows: Lap joint
The best and strongest
The parts overlap, giving a large bonded area. A common guide is an overlap of at least **three times the thickness of the thinner part**. Done well, the joint is then stronger than the thinner part.
Socket (sleeve) joint
Very good
A lap joint wrapped round a tube: the tube slides into a fitting. Pipe fittings are made to give the right gap.
Scarf joint
Fair
The edges are cut at a long slope and overlapped, which gives more area than a butt joint
Butt joint
Weak
Only the thin edges meet, so the bonded area is small. Avoid it, or braze weld it with a V preparation, or add a sleeve or strap.
Tee joint
Fair
Brazed with a fillet each side, often with brass rod

blocks.p: For silver brazing, the gap (also called the **clearance**) must be **small and even**: typically about 0.05–0.15 mm, a fraction of a millimetre, as the filler maker says. Brass rod can bridge somewhat wider gaps, and braze welding fills a V-groove of several millimetres.

head: Gap
What happens
rows: Too tight, or the parts forced together
The filler cannot get in, so the joint is left part-filled
Right: small and even
Capillary action pulls the filler right through; a thin, strong layer forms
Too wide or uneven
Capillary action is weak, the filler runs out or leaves voids, much more filler is used, and the joint is weaker

blocks.note: Copper tube and fittings are made to give the right capillary gap. A tube end that is dented, oval or burred spoils that gap: cut the damaged part off rather than force it in.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Grease, oil, paint, rust and oxide stop the filler wetting and bonding. Clean every surface the filler must touch, back to **bright metal**:

ul: Copper and brass: emery cloth, a fine abrasive pad, fine wire wool or a fitting brush.
Steel: a wire brush, emery cloth or a file; grind off heavy rust, scale or paint.
Wipe off oil and grease with a clean rag and a suitable solvent, and let it dry.
Do not touch cleaned surfaces with your fingers or greasy gloves.
Flux and braze soon after cleaning, before a new oxide forms.

blocks.note: In humid, salty air near the coast, clean copper and steel tarnish within hours. Clean just before you flux and braze, not the day before.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Preparing a copper tube and fitting

flow: Measure and mark the tube, allowing for the depth it goes into each fitting
Cut it square with a tube cutter
Remove the burr inside and outside with a deburring tool: a burr stops the tube going fully home and narrows the bore
Check that the tube is round and slides into the socket with a small, even gap
Clean the outside of the tube end and the inside of the socket to bright metal
Brush a thin coat of flux on the tube end, push it fully home and turn it to spread the flux
Support the parts so they stay in line and cannot move while they are heated

ul: Use clamps, binding wire, a jig, or firebricks shaped to hold the work, so the parts keep their line and gap while they are heated.
Better still, design the parts to hold themselves: a push fit, a crimp or a small tab.
Keep big clamps back from the joint: a heavy clamp draws heat away and stops the joint reaching temperature.
Allow for the parts expanding as they heat, and make sure nothing can fall when the filler is liquid.
Read the **drawing and job sheet**: the parent metals, sizes, joint types, and whether the joint must be strong, leak-tight or neat.
Choose the process: silver brazing for copper pipe and small close-fitting parts; brass brazing for steel.
Choose a filler that melts well below the parent metal, and a flux that suits both the filler and the metal. Read their labels and safety data sheets.
Choose the torch and nozzle size for the thickness and the size of the job.
Collect the tools: tube cutter, deburring tool, cleaning materials, flux brush, clamps, firebricks and tongs.
Prepare the area: ventilation or extraction, burnables cleared, extinguisher at hand, then check the gas equipment.
Ask your instructor about anything that is not clear before you start.

blocks.note: **Heat the parent metal, not the rod.** The hot parts must melt the filler. If the flame melts the rod, the drops land on metal that is too cold and sit there in balls.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Heat the **whole joint area**, not one spot. Keep the flame **moving** so the heat spreads evenly with no hot spots.
Both parts must reach brazing heat **at the same time**. Filler only flows where the metal is hot enough.
Melted filler flows **towards the heat**. Use this: heat the far side of a joint to draw the filler right through it.
A **thick or heavy** part takes longer to heat and draws heat away from the joint, so it needs more of the flame. A thin part heats quickly and is easily overheated.
**Copper** carries heat away much faster than steel, so a copper part needs more heat than a steel part of the same size.
Watch the **flux**: it tells you when the joint is ready and warns you when you are overheating.

head: Situation
Where to put most of the heat
rows: Thin tube into a heavy fitting
Warm the tube briefly, then put most of the heat on the heavy fitting, sweeping round it
Thin sheet onto a thick bar
On the bar, letting the heat flow into the sheet; pass the flame only briefly over the sheet
Copper part joined to a steel part
More on the copper, because it carries heat away faster
A long lap seam
Preheat a length of the seam, then braze along it steadily, keeping the flame just ahead of the filler

blocks.h: Silver brazing a copper socket joint

flow: Light the torch and set a neutral or slightly reducing (soft) flame, sized to suit the fitting
Heat the tube close to the fitting for a few seconds
Move the flame onto the fitting, sweeping it round so that all sides heat evenly
Watch the flux: it bubbles, then turns clear and runs like water
Touch the rod to the joint at the mouth of the socket, on the side away from the flame, and let the hot metal melt it
Feed the rod until a thin, bright ring of filler shows all round the mouth; do not flood the joint
Take the flame away and hold the joint still until the filler has set
Let it cool, then wash and brush off the flux
Clean the steel to bright metal; set up the lap joint with the overlap the drawing gives, on firebricks, clamped
Set the flame your instructor gives for brass rod, often neutral to slightly oxidising
Heat the end of the rod and dip it in the flux, or use a flux-coated rod; flux the joint
Heat the start of the joint until the steel glows red (your instructor will show you the colour) and the flux has melted and spread
Touch the rod to the hot steel: when the brass runs out in a thin film, move steadily along the joint, adding rod
Keep most of the heat on the steel just ahead of the filler; if white smoke rises, the joint is too hot
Finish the joint, take the flame away and keep the parts still until the brass has set

blocks.note: In braze welding, the first thin film of brass that runs over the hot steel is called **tinning**. If the brass runs out freely like water, the steel is at the right heat. If it balls up, the steel is too cold. If it boils and gives off white smoke, the steel is too hot.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Signs of too little and too much heat

head: Too little heat
Too much heat
rows: Flux stays white or crusty and does not turn clear
The filler balls up on the surface and will not run into the joint
The filler melts only where the flame touches it
Flux burns dark green or black and stops working
Heavy oxide forms and the filler stops flowing
White zinc smoke from brass rod, and a porous, pitted filler
Thin parent metal sags or melts

ul: As the filler cools, it passes through a soft, mushy stage before it goes solid. If the parts move then, the joint cracks or is left weak.
Hold the parts still, or leave them in their clamps, until the filler has set.

Do not drop hot work into cold water. Once the filler has set and the colour has gone, your instructor may let you put a copper or brass part into **hot water** to help lift the flux. Never quench steel parts, or joints between two different metals.
Most flux residue is **corrosive**. Left on, it eats into the metal (often showing as a green crust on copper), spoils paint and can hide faults.
Silver brazing flux dissolves in **hot water**: soak the part and scrub it with a stiff brush.
Borax-type residue is hard and glassy: break it off lightly and wire-brush it, then wash the part in hot water.
On air-conditioning and refrigeration lines, clean the outside only and keep water out of the pipe.
Treat every brazed part as hot. Pick it up with tongs or pliers.
Mark hot work HOT with soapstone or chalk, and leave it to cool in a safe place where no one will touch it.
Copper carries heat a long way: a pipe can be too hot to hold half a metre from the joint.

blocks.h: What a good joint looks like

head: Check
A good joint
rows: Fillet
A smooth, even, slightly hollow (concave) fillet of filler showing all the way round a socket, or along both edges of a lap
Fill
Filler drawn right through the joint, showing at the far side where you can see it
Surface
No lumps or balls of filler, no burnt black flux, no cracks and no pinholes
Parent metal
Not melted, sagged or heavily scaled
Cleanliness
All flux residue washed off
Size and line
Parts in line and square; sizes as the drawing says

head: Fault
What you see
Main causes
How to prevent it
rows: Voids (lack of fill)
Gaps or holes inside the joint where the filler did not reach; often found only in a peel test or by a leak
Dirty or oxidised surfaces
Gap too wide, too tight or uneven
Uneven heating: part of the joint too cold
Not enough flux or filler
Clean to bright metal
Set a small, even gap
Heat the whole joint evenly
Enough flux and filler
Filler balling
Round beads of filler sitting on the surface, not wetted or drawn in
Parent metal too cold
Rod melted in the flame instead of by the work
Oxide or dirt; no flux
Heat the parts until the flux runs clear
Let the hot work melt the rod
Clean and flux properly
Overheating
Burnt black flux, heavy oxide, rough sluggish filler; white smoke and pitted filler with brass; melted parent metal
Flame too large or too hot
Flame held still on one spot
Heating for too long
Right nozzle and flame
Keep the flame moving
Watch the flux and stop when it is ready
Cracks
Fine lines in the filler or along the edge of the joint
Parts moved while the filler was setting
Quenching hot work
Copper-phosphorus filler used on steel
Support the parts and keep them still
Let the joint cool naturally
Use the right filler
Flux inclusions
Pockets of trapped flux inside the joint
Too much flux
Gap too wide
Filler fed from both sides, trapping flux in the middle
Thin coat of flux
Correct gap
Feed from one side and draw the filler through with the heat
Excess filler
Lumps, runs and drips on the surface or inside the pipe
Too much rod fed in
Flux spread where filler is not wanted
Overheating spreading the filler
Feed only until the ring or fillet is complete
Flux only where needed
Right heat
Corrosion afterwards
Green or white crust forming round the joint days or weeks later
Flux residue not washed off
Wash and scrub off all flux after brazing

ul: **Visual inspection** of every joint, after the flux is washed off.

**Water test** for pipework: fill the system with water, let out the air, bring it to the test pressure the job sets, hold it for the time the job sets (the Centre's practical uses 10 minutes), and check every joint for drips with a dry cloth.

**Peel test**: a destructive test on a sample lap joint. Cut a strip across the joint and peel the two pieces apart in a vice. Bright filler over most of the overlap shows good flow; dry, dark patches are voids where the filler did not reach.
Air-conditioning and refrigeration lines are pressure-tested with dry nitrogen and leak-checked by a qualified technician.

blocks.note: Never pressure-test a pipe or a system with oxygen or a fuel gas. Oxygen meeting oil or grease inside a system can cause an explosion.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Close the torch valves in the order the torch maker gives, and hang the torch up away from the cylinders
Close both cylinder valves
Open the oxygen torch valve to let the gas out of the oxygen hose and regulator, then close it; do the same for the fuel gas, one gas at a time, in a ventilated place away from flames
Check that all the gauges read zero
Wind out both regulator adjusting screws until they are loose
Coil the hoses loosely, with no kinks, and hang them off the floor away from hot metal and oil

blocks.p: For an **air-LPG torch**, close the cylinder valve first and let the flame burn the gas out of the hose until it goes out, then close the torch valve.

ul: Leave brazed parts to cool in a safe place, marked HOT.
Put the lids back on flux pots, and return fillers to the store in their labelled packets.
Hand short ends of silver alloy back as your instructor says: they are valuable.
Put rod ends, flux scraps and dirty rags in the bins the Centre's rules name. Never wash flux or waste into a drain, and never burn waste on the hearth.
Clean the bench and the hearth, and check the whole area for smouldering before you leave.

head: What to report
Examples
What to do
rows: Faulty gas equipment
A cracked or burnt hose, a fitting that bubbles, a regulator whose working gauge keeps creeping up with the torch closed, a backfiring nozzle, a flashback
Shut it down, tag it DO NOT USE, and tell your instructor. Do not repair regulators or arrestors yourself.
Injuries
Burns, flux in the eye, symptoms of metal fume fever
First aid, tell your instructor, record it in the accident book
Near misses
A small fire, a flashback, a hose found lying across hot metal
Report it so the cause is found and fixed
Materials
Cadmium-bearing filler in the store, flux that has dried out, a filler packet with no label
Report it so it is removed, replaced or relabelled
Your job
Joints that failed the water test, faults you could not correct, the job finished
Tell your instructor and fill in the job card

blocks.note: Reporting a fault is not getting someone into trouble. A leaking fitting or a creeping regulator reported today is a fire or an explosion prevented tomorrow.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain how brazing differs from welding and from soft soldering, including the 450 °C dividing line.
I can explain capillary action and wetting, and what a joint needs for them to work.
I can say when to use silver brazing, brass brazing and braze welding.
I can name the hazards of brazing, including flux, zinc and cadmium fumes, and say how to control each one.
I can choose and check my PPE, including goggles of about shade 3 to 5.
I can set up, leak-test and purge an oxy-acetylene set, and say why each safety device is fitted.
I can light the torch safely and set a carburising, neutral or oxidising flame, and say which one suits each job.
I can say what to do after a backfire or a flashback.
I can choose a filler and a flux for copper, brass and steel, and say why copper-phosphorus filler is never used on steel.
I can read the changes in silver brazing flux as the joint heats up.
I can design or check a lap or socket joint with the right overlap and gap.
I can cut, deburr, clean, flux and hold a copper tube joint ready for brazing.
I can heat a joint evenly, put more heat on the heavier part, and let the hot work melt the filler.
I can silver braze a copper socket joint and brass braze a lap joint in thin steel.
I can wash off flux and inspect a brazed joint, naming faults with their causes and cures.
I can carry out a water test and a peel test and say what each shows.
I can shut down the gas equipment, store materials, dispose of waste and report faults.

terms: Backfire
A loud pop as the flame goes into the nozzle and goes out or relights
Borax
A white compound of boron that is the base of many brass brazing fluxes
Braze welding
Building up a fillet or filling a groove with brass rod, like a weld bead, without relying on capillary flow; also called bronze welding
Brazing
Joining metals with a filler that melts above about 450 °C but below the parent metal
Cadmium
A metal in some older silver brazing alloys; its fume is very toxic
Capillary action
The pull that draws a liquid into a narrow gap between two close surfaces
Carburising flame
A flame with extra acetylene, showing a white feather round the inner cone
Check valve
A one-way valve where each hose joins the torch; also called a non-return valve
Clearance
The gap between the two surfaces of a brazed joint
Copper-phosphorus filler
A brazing filler that acts as its own flux on copper; never used on steel
Filler metal
The metal that is melted into a brazed joint to fill and join it
Flashback
A flame burning back inside the torch towards the hoses, with a squeal or hiss
Flashback arrestor
A safety device at the regulator outlet that stops a flame reaching the cylinder
Flux
A paste or powder that removes and prevents oxide so the filler can wet the metal
Inner cone
The small, bright inner part of an oxy-acetylene flame
Lap joint
A joint where the parts overlap; the strongest brazed joint
LPG
Liquefied petroleum gas (propane or butane), the fuel of air-fuel torches; heavier than air
Metal fume fever
A flu-like illness from breathing zinc or other metal fume
Neutral flame
A flame with a clear, rounded inner cone and no feather
Oxidising flame
A flame with extra oxygen: a short, pointed inner cone and a hiss
Parent metal
The metal of the parts being joined; also called the base metal
Peel test
Peeling a sample lap joint apart to see how far the filler ran
Purging
Letting each gas through its hose briefly to clear out air or mixed gas before lighting
Regulator
The device that lowers the cylinder pressure to a steady working pressure
Safety data sheet (SDS)
The supplier's sheet giving a product's hazards and how to handle it safely
Silver soldering
The trade name for silver brazing
Soft soldering
Joining with a filler that melts below about 450 °C
Spark lighter
The flint tool used to light a gas torch
Tinning
The first thin film of filler that runs over the hot surface
Voids
Gaps or holes in a brazed joint where the filler did not fill it
Wetting
Melted filler spreading evenly over clean metal and sticking to it

c1.title: Air-conditioning lines at a guest house in Ocho Rios
c1.text: Shanice, a Level 2 trainee on work experience with an air-conditioning technician, is helping to fit a split unit at a guest house in Ocho Rios, St Ann. The copper refrigerant lines must be silver brazed to the brass service valves on the outdoor unit; the valves have rubber seals inside. The technician hands her copper-phosphorus rod. One joint is about 30 cm from a varnished wooden window frame.

c2.title: Chair frames in Spanish Town
c2.text: Devon runs a small shop in Spanish Town, St Catherine, that repairs steel school furniture. A batch of chairs have legs of thin-wall steel tube (1.2 mm wall) that have cracked away from the seat frames, which still carry old paint and rust. Devon and Alicia, a trainee, are brass brazing the repairs with an oxy-acetylene set.

c3.title: A solar water heater in Mandeville
c3.text: Tajay, an apprentice plumber, is silver soldering 22 mm copper pipe to connect a solar water heater on a house in Mandeville, Manchester. He cuts some tube ends with a hacksaw. On his first joint he points the flame at the rod and lets the drops fall onto the fitting. His supervisor gives him copper-phosphorus rod for the copper-to-copper joints.

c4.title: Peel tests at the Centre
c4.text: At a training centre in Kingston, trainees have brass brazed lap joints in 1.5 mm mild steel sheet and peeled sample strips apart in the vice. Nadine's strip shows filler only about 3 mm into a 10 mm overlap, with dry, dark patches beyond it. Omar's top sheet has a melted notch at its edge. Kerry-Ann lifted her joint off the firebricks with tongs straight after the brass flowed, and it has a fine crack along the edge of the filler.

c5.title: Setting up the brazing bay in Montego Bay
c5.text: Rohan is setting up the oxy-acetylene set in the brazing bay of a training centre in Montego Bay, St James. A new acetylene cylinder was delivered lying on its side on the back of a truck. After he has set the pressures and closed the torch valves, he notices that the acetylene working gauge keeps creeping slowly upwards.

questions.q: Shanice is about to braze a copper line to a brass valve with the copper-phosphorus rod. What else does this joint need?
o: A suitable brazing flux, because brass is in the joint
Nothing extra: copper-phosphorus rod needs no flux on any metal
A strongly oxidising flame, which does the job of the flux
A coat of soft-solder flux to make the rod flow further
questions.why: Copper-phosphorus filler acts as its own flux only on copper to copper. As soon as brass or another metal is in the joint, a suitable flux is needed or the filler will not wet the brass.

questions.q: How should Shanice protect the rubber seals inside the brass valve while she brazes?
o: Braze quickly with a large flame aimed straight at the valve body
Wrap the valve body in a wet rag and keep the flame on the joint
Take the valve off and braze it on the bench, then refit it later
Heat the whole valve first so that it expands evenly with the line
questions.why: A wet rag (or a heat-absorbing paste) soaks up heat that would travel along the valve body to the seals. The flame stays on the joint, not on the valve body.

questions.q: What should be done about the wooden window frame before the nearby joint is brazed?
o: Wet the frame with water and carry on, since wood cannot burn when damp
Nothing, as long as she keeps the inner cone pointing at the copper
Put a heat shield behind the joint and keep an extinguisher by her
Ask the owner to open the window so the heat can escape outside
questions.why: The flame and hot copper can scorch or ignite varnished wood behind the joint. A heat shield stops the heat reaching it, and an extinguisher must be at hand; the area is checked again before leaving.

questions.q: When the lines are finished, how should they be tested for leaks?
o: Fill them with oxygen and brush soapy water on every joint
Light the torch near each joint and watch the flame for a flicker
Fill them with water and leave them overnight to check for drips
Have the technician pressure-test them with dry nitrogen
questions.why: Refrigerant lines are tested with dry nitrogen by a qualified technician. Oxygen must never be used because it can explode with oil in the system, and water must be kept out of refrigerant lines.

questions.q: The shop owner asks why the cracked legs are brazed rather than fusion welded. What is the best reason?
o: The finished joint will never need painting or rust protection
Less heat goes in, so the thin tube is less likely to burn through
The brass melts deeper into the tube walls, giving a stronger joint
There is no need to clean off the old paint and rust beforehand
questions.why: In brazing the parent metal does not melt, so far less heat goes into the thin 1.2 mm wall. There is less risk of burning through and less distortion; cleaning is still essential.

questions.q: What must Alicia do about the old paint and rust before she brazes?
o: Clean them off to bright metal around the whole joint area
Leave them on, because the flux will burn them away
Paint over them with flux so that the brass can run underneath
Scrape off only the loose flakes and braze over the rest
questions.why: Paint and rust stop the brass wetting and bonding, and burning paint gives off fumes. Flux removes thin oxide only; it cannot clean away paint or rust.

questions.q: While brazing, Alicia sees white smoke rising from the joint and the brass looks pitted. What does it tell her?
o: The steel is too cold, so she should hold the flame still on the joint
The flux is working well and the joint is nearly finished
The rod is damp and should be dried in a rod oven
The joint is overheating and zinc is boiling off the brass
questions.why: White smoke is zinc oxide from overheated brass. It leaves porous filler and gives off fume that causes metal fume fever, so she reduces the heat and keeps her face out of it.

questions.q: Which flux should Devon use with the brass rods on the steel tube?
o: The white silver brazing paste, as it works on any metal
No flux, since cleaned steel tube does not need any
A borax-type brazing flux, or flux-coated brass rods
A plumbing soldering flux, because it works at a lower heat
questions.why: Brass rod melts at about 870–900 °C, so it needs a flux that works at that heat, such as a borax-type flux. Silver brazing and soldering fluxes are made for lower temperatures and break down.

questions.q: On his first joint, the filler sat in round beads on the fitting and did not run in. What should Tajay change?
o: Heat the parts until the flux runs clear and let them melt the rod
Use a bigger nozzle and keep the flame on the rod so it melts faster
Add more flux on top of the beads and heat the beads again
Push the tube further into the fitting so that the gap closes up
questions.why: The filler balled because the parent metal was too cold to be wetted. When the parts are hot enough to melt the rod themselves, capillary action draws the filler into the joint.

questions.q: One hacksawn tube end is slightly out of square with a burr inside. What should Tajay do before fitting it?
o: Fit it as it is, because the filler will fill the uneven gap
Put extra flux on the burr so that the filler can flow over it
Recut it square with a tube cutter and remove the burr
Hammer the end round on the bench until it slides in tightly
questions.why: An end that is out of square or burred stops the tube going fully home, spoils the even capillary gap and narrows the bore. A square, deburred end gives the right fit.

questions.q: Tajay asks why the copper-phosphorus rod needs no flux on these copper joints. What is the answer?
o: The silver in the rod stops any oxide forming on hot copper
The phosphorus in the rod cleans the copper oxide as it melts
Copper does not form any oxide when it is heated with a flame
The rod melts below 450 °C, so oxide never has time to form
questions.why: Phosphorus in the filler acts as a flux on copper, so copper-to-copper joints need none. It does not work on brass or steel, and these rods are never used on steel.

questions.q: Tajay sees green, crusty deposits round a joint made on another job a few weeks earlier. What is the most likely cause?
o: The joint gap was too small for the filler to enter
Flux residue that was not washed off after brazing
The copper-phosphorus rod was used without any flux
The pipe was water-tested before the joint had cooled
questions.why: Most flux residue is corrosive. Left on the joint it attacks the copper, often as a green crust, so it is soaked and scrubbed off with hot water after every job.

questions.q: What does Nadine's peel test show, and what is the most likely cause?
o: Voids: the overlap was not all hot enough, or not clean
Overheating: too much heat drove the filler out of the lap
A good joint: 3 mm of filler is all a lap joint needs
Cracking: the joint was moved before the filler set
questions.why: Dry, dark patches beyond the filler are voids where it never reached. Filler only flows where the metal is clean, fluxed and at brazing heat, so the whole overlap must be heated evenly.

questions.q: What most likely caused the melted notch in the edge of Omar's top sheet?
o: The brass rod was fed in too slowly along the joint
The steel was cleaned too much and became too thin
The inner cone was held on the thin edge for too long
The firebricks drew too much heat out of the bottom sheet
questions.why: A thin edge heats much faster than the plate below it. Holding the inner cone on it melts it; most of the heat should go to the bottom sheet, with the flame kept moving.

questions.q: Why did Kerry-Ann's joint crack?
o: The brass was the wrong alloy for joining steel sheet
The overlap was too long for the thickness of sheet
The flame was set slightly oxidising for the brass rod
It was moved while the brass was still setting
questions.why: Brass passes through a soft, mushy stage as it cools. Moving the joint then tears the filler, so the parts are kept still until it has set.

questions.q: Using the common rule of three times the thinner part, what is the least overlap for a lap joint between 1.2 mm and 2 mm sheet?
o: 2.4 mm
3.6 mm
6.0 mm
9.6 mm
questions.why: The rule uses the thinner part: 3 × 1.2 mm = 3.6 mm. Using the thicker sheet (6 mm) or adding the two thicknesses gives the wrong answer; the drawing may ask for more.

questions.q: What should Rohan do with the acetylene cylinder that arrived lying on its side?
o: Use it at once, but open the valve fully so any acetone blows out
Lay it flat beside the bay so that it cannot fall over while in use
Stand it upright and wait the time the supplier gives before use
Stand it up and rock it a few times to mix the acetone back in
questions.why: Lying down lets acetone reach the valve, where it can come out with the gas and damage the equipment. Standing it upright for the time the supplier gives lets the acetone settle back.

questions.q: The acetylene working gauge keeps creeping up with the torch valves closed. What should Rohan do?
o: Shut off the cylinder, tag the regulator out and report it
Wind the adjusting screw in further until the needle stops moving
Carry on, since a little creep is normal on a newly fitted cylinder
Light the torch at once so that the extra pressure is used up
questions.why: A creeping working gauge means the regulator is leaking past its seat, so pressure can build above the safe limit. The set is shut down, the regulator tagged out and reported; regulators are not repaired by trainees.

questions.q: Rohan's leak test shows bubbles at the fuel hose connection on the regulator. What should he do?
o: Wrap tape round the connection and test it again
Close the cylinder valves, bleed the gas, then fix and retest
Turn the fuel pressure down until the bubbles become smaller
Light the torch and use it, since the leak is outside the torch
questions.why: A fuel gas leak can catch fire or explode. The gas is shut off and bled before the joint is tightened or the part replaced, and it is tested again before use; tape is never used on gas fittings.

questions.q: In the store you find a packet of silver brazing rod marked "contains cadmium". What should you do?
o: Use it outdoors, where the fumes can blow away
Use it only for small joints that need little filler
Use it with a larger flame so it melts more quickly
Do not use it; hand it to your instructor
questions.why: Cadmium fume is very toxic and can cause severe lung damage, even from a short exposure. Only cadmium-free fillers are used; old stock is handed in for safe disposal.
